lessons.title: One-Pass and Multi-Pass Milling Systems
lessons.body:
In rice milling, a 'pass' means one trip through a machine that removes some bran or polishes the grain. A one-pass system uses a single machine to dehusk, whiten, and polish in one go. This is common in small African mills where a farmer brings 100â200 kg of paddy and wants quick results. A typical one-pass mill, like the popular Engelberg or similar steel huller, can process 200â500 kg per hour. It's cheap (costing $500â$2,000) and easy to operate, but the rice often breaks more, and the bran is mixed with husk, making it less valuable for oil extraction or animal feed.

A multi-pass system uses two or more machines: a dehusker (rubber roller), a paddy separator, a whitener (abrasive or friction), a polisher, and sometimes a grader. Each machine does one job well. For example, a 2-pass system might have a dehusker and a whitener; a 3-pass system adds a polisher. Multi-pass mills cost more ($5,000â$50,000) but produce higher head rice yield (50â60% whole kernels) and cleaner bran. In Nigeria, Tanzania, and Kenya, medium-scale mills (1â2 tonnes/hour) usually use multi-pass systems to meet market demand for premium rice.

When choosing a system, consider your volume and market. If you mill less than 500 kg per day for local customers, a one-pass mill is fine. If you sell to supermarkets or export, invest in multi-pass. Also, check power supply: one-pass mills often run on a 10â15 HP diesel engine, while multi-pass lines need 30â50 HP or three-phase electricity. Many African entrepreneurs start with a one-pass mill, then add a dehusker and whitener as profits grow. Remember, proper paddy cleaning (destoning, dehusking) before milling reduces wear and breakage in both systems.

lessons.title: Vertical and Horizontal Milling Machines
lessons.body:
Rice milling machines come in two main orientations: vertical and horizontal. The orientation affects how the grain moves through the whitening chamber, how much pressure is applied, and how easy it is to maintain. A vertical milling machine has a vertical shaft with abrasive rollers or friction discs. The paddy or brown rice enters at the top and falls down by gravity, passing between the rollers and a screen. This design is common in small to medium mills across Africa because it takes less floor space and uses gravity to help move the grain. Examples include the VTA (vertical abrasive) whitener, often used in 1â2 tonne/hour mills. Vertical machines are easier to clean and require less power (10â20 HP) because they don't need to push grain horizontally against gravity.

A horizontal milling machine has a horizontal shaft, and the grain is moved along by a screw conveyor or by the rotation of the roller. The most common horizontal type is the friction whitener, where a steel roller rotates inside a perforated screen. The grain is pushed against the screen, creating friction that removes bran. Horizontal machines can handle higher capacities (2â10 tonnes/hour) and are often used in large commercial mills. However, they need more floor space and more power (30â100 HP). They also generate more heat, which can cause broken grains if not controlled.

In practice, many African mills use a combination: a vertical dehusker (rubber roller) followed by a horizontal friction whitener. When choosing, consider your power source and maintenance skills. Vertical machines have fewer moving parts and are easier to repair with local tools. Horizontal machines may need imported bearings and belts. If you are off-grid, a vertical machine with a diesel engine is a smart choice. If you have three-phase electricity and mill over 2 tonnes per hour, horizontal machines give better throughput. Always check that spare parts (screens, rollers) are available locally or can be ordered from suppliers in Kenya, Nigeria, or South Africa.

lessons.title: Abrasive and Friction Whitening Techniques
lessons.body:
Whitening is the process of removing the bran layer from brown rice to get white rice. There are two main techniques: abrasive whitening and friction whitening. Abrasive whitening uses a rotating abrasive stone or roller (often made of emery or carborundum) that scrapes the bran off the grain. The grain is held against the stone by a screen or pressure gate. This method is gentle and works well for long-grain rice, as it produces less broken kernels. Abrasive whitening is common in vertical machines and is ideal for African rice varieties that are often slender and fragile. A typical abrasive whitener might remove 4â6% of the grain weight as bran in one pass, and you can adjust the pressure to control the degree of milling.

Friction whitening uses a steel roller that spins at high speed inside a perforated screen. The grain rubs against itself and the screen, and the friction generates heat that loosens the bran. This method is more aggressive and can remove bran faster, but it also creates more broken grains and heat. Friction whitening is often used in horizontal machines for higher capacity. In many African mills, a combination is used: first an abrasive pass to remove most bran, then a friction pass to polish the rice to a shine. This two-step approach balances yield and quality.

To get the best results, adjust the pressure and speed. For abrasive whiteners, keep the stone clean and dressed (sharpened) every 100â200 hours of operation. For friction whiteners, monitor the temperature; if the rice feels hot, reduce the feed rate or increase the air flow. In rural areas, you can test the degree of milling by rubbing a few grains with your fingers: if the bran comes off easily, you're not milling enough; if the grain cracks, you're milling too hard. Remember, over-milling wastes rice and reduces profits. Aim for a whiteness that meets your market's preference, often around 8â10% bran removal for local markets, but up to 12% for premium export.

lessons.title: Milling Machine Components and Adjustments
lessons.body:
A rice milling machine is made up of several key components that work together. The main parts are: the hopper (where paddy or brown rice is fed), the feeding mechanism (often a screw or vibratory feeder), the milling chamber (where whitening happens), the screen (which holds the grain and lets bran escape), the pressure gate or brake (which controls the resistance and thus the degree of milling), the discharge chute (where milled rice exits), and the drive system (motor, belts, pulleys). Understanding these parts helps you operate and maintain the machine properly.

Adjustments are critical for good milling. The pressure gate is the most important: opening it reduces pressure, giving less milling and more whole grains; closing it increases pressure, removing more bran but risking breakage. Start with a medium setting and adjust based on the rice you're milling. The feed rate also matters: if you feed too fast, the chamber overloads and rice breaks; too slow, and you waste capacity. Aim for a steady, full flow. The clearance between the roller and screen should be set according to the manufacturer's manualâusually 10â15 mm for abrasive whiteners, less for friction. Check this with a feeler gauge.

In Africa, where power can fluctuate, belt tension is often overlooked. Loose belts slip and reduce speed, leading to poor milling. Check belts weekly and tighten or replace as needed. Also, the screen wears out: holes get enlarged, letting whole grains escape. Inspect screens every 100 hours and replace when holes exceed 2 mm. Lubricate bearings regularly with grease (every 50â100 hours) to prevent overheating. Keep a logbook of adjustments and maintenance. Many mills fail because operators don't record what settings work best for different rice varieties. Train your staff on these basics: a well-adjusted machine can increase head rice yield by 5â10%, which is real money.

lessons.title: Process Flow Diagrams for Rice Mills
lessons.body:
A process flow diagram (PFD) is a simple drawing that shows the steps rice goes through from paddy to polished rice. It helps you design a mill, train workers, and spot bottlenecks. For a small one-pass mill, the PFD is short: paddy â cleaning (destoner, sieve) â dehusking (if separate) â milling (whitening) â polishing â grading â bagging. But most African mills use multi-pass systems, so the PFD is longer. A typical 2-tonne/hour mill might have: paddy intake â pre-cleaning (remove straw, stones) â dehusking (rubber roll) â paddy separation (separate brown rice from unhulled paddy) â whitening (abrasive) â polishing (friction) â grading (broken, head rice) â bagging. Each step has equipment and a purpose.

Drawing a PFD is easy. Use boxes for machines, arrows for flow, and label each box. For example, start with 'Paddy Hopper' â 'Destoner' â 'Rubber Roll Dehusker' â 'Paddy Separator' â 'Abrasive Whitener' â 'Friction Polisher' â 'Grading Screen' â 'Bagging'. Include bypass lines for re-milling broken rice. Also note the by-products: husk goes to a collector (for fuel or animal bedding), bran goes to a bin (for oil extraction or feed). In many African mills, husk is burned to power the mill or make briquettes, and bran is sold to livestock farmers.

A good PFD helps you calculate capacity at each stage. For instance, if your dehusker can handle 2 tonnes/hour but your whitener only 1.5 tonnes/hour, you have a bottleneck. You can then add a second whitener or slow the feed. Use the PFD to plan maintenance: if a machine breaks, you know which steps are affected. Train your workers to understand the PFD so they can troubleshoot. In Kenya and Nigeria, many millers use simple hand-drawn PFDs on cardboard, which is fineâthe key is to have a clear, logical flow. Always keep the PFD updated when you add or change equipment.

lessons.title: Capacity and Efficiency Calculations
lessons.body:
Knowing your mill's capacity and efficiency is essential for profit. Capacity is how much paddy you can process per hour, usually measured in tonnes per hour (t/h) or kilograms per hour (kg/h). Efficiency is the percentage of good head rice you get from the paddy. To calculate capacity, weigh the paddy you mill in one hour. For example, if you mill 500 kg of paddy in one hour, your capacity is 0.5 t/h. But capacity depends on the rice variety and moisture: wet paddy (above 14% moisture) mills slower and breaks more. Always mill dry paddy (12â14% moisture) for best results.

Efficiency is calculated as: (weight of head rice / weight of paddy) Ã 100. Head rice is whole kernels, not broken. Suppose you start with 100 kg paddy and get 55 kg head rice, 15 kg broken, 20 kg bran, and 10 kg husk. Your head rice yield is 55%. Good mills achieve 60â65% for local varieties, but many small African mills get only 40â50% due to poor adjustment. To improve, reduce broken rice by setting the pressure gate correctly and maintaining sharp abrasive stones. Also, pre-clean paddy thoroughly: stones and straw cause breakage.

Another key metric is milling recovery: total milled rice (head + broken) divided by paddy weight. If you get 70 kg milled rice from 100 kg paddy, recovery is 70%. But head rice is more valuable. Track your numbers daily. For a 1 t/h mill running 8 hours, you process 8 tonnes paddy. At 55% head rice, you get 4.4 tonnes head rice. If you sell head rice at $0.80/kg and broken at $0.40/kg, revenue = (4.4Ã800) + (1.2Ã400) = $3,520 + $480 = $4,000. If you improve head rice to 60%, you get 4.8 tonnes head rice and 0.8 tonnes broken: revenue = (4.8Ã800) + (0.8Ã400) = $3,840 + $320 = $4,160. That's $160 extra per dayâover $40,000 a year! So small improvements in efficiency mean big money. Use a simple notebook to record daily paddy input, head rice, broken, bran, and husk. Calculate your efficiency weekly and adjust your machine accordingly.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Rice Milling Systems and Equipment

This practical reference consolidates the core engineering and business knowledge you need to select, run, and troubleshoot a rice mill in an African context. Whether you are a smallholder cooperative in Tanzania running a single-pass mill, or an SME in Nigeria operating a multi-pass plant, the goal is the same: maximise head rice recovery, minimise broken grains, and keep the cost per tonne of milled rice as low as possible. Every technical decision here has a direct effect on your margin.

Rice milling is not just a mechanical process â it is a business process. In West Africa, post-harvest losses in rice can reach 15â30%, and much of that loss happens at the milling stage. A well-adjusted mill can recover 5â10 percentage points more head rice than a poorly maintained one. On a 2-tonne-per-hour mill running 1,000 hours per year, that difference is worth tens of thousands of dollars in additional saleable rice. This module gives you the reference data, diagrams, and checklists to capture that value.

One-Pass vs Multi-Pass Milling Systems

A one-pass mill (often called a "single-pass" or "steel huller" mill) removes the husk and bran in a single machine, typically a combined rubber-roll huller and friction whitener. These are common across Africa because they are cheap, portable, and easy to operate. However, they produce high broken-grain percentages (often 20â35% broken) and lower head rice recovery. They are best suited for local consumption markets where broken rice is acceptable, or for parboiled rice which is more resistant to breakage.

A multi-pass mill separates the operations: dehusking (rubber roll), paddy separation, whitening (2â3 passes of abrasive and friction), polishing, and grading. This produces higher head rice recovery (55â65% of paddy) and better market prices. The trade-off is higher capital cost, more maintenance, and the need for skilled operators. For any business targeting urban markets, supermarkets, or export, multi-pass is the standard.

Vertical and Horizontal Milling Machines

Horizontal milling machines use a horizontal shaft to drive the abrasive or friction cylinder. They are the traditional design found in many older African mills. They are robust and easy to repair locally, but they tend to produce more broken grains because the grain residence time is uneven and the pressure distribution is less controlled.

Vertical milling machines (vertical shaft whitening) have become the industry standard. The grain moves downward by gravity, giving more uniform residence time, lower broken-grain percentages, and better heat dissipation. Vertical machines are also more compact and easier to integrate into multi-pass layouts. For a new investment in Africa, vertical abrasive-friction machines (e.g., from Chinese, Indian, or Turkish manufacturers) are generally the better choice, though spare parts availability must be verified before purchase.

Abrasive and Friction Whitening Techniques

Whitening removes the bran layer. Two mechanisms are used:

  • Abrasive whitening: a rotating abrasive stone (carborundum) scrapes the bran off the grain surface. It is effective for the first whitening pass and works well on parboiled rice. It generates less heat but wears the stone, which must be dressed and replaced.
  • Friction whitening: grains rub against each other under pressure inside a perforated screen cylinder. This is used in later passes to polish the grain and remove remaining bran. It generates more heat and requires careful pressure adjustment to avoid breaking grains.

Most multi-pass mills use a sequence: abrasive first pass â friction second pass â friction/water polish third pass. The exact configuration depends on the paddy variety, moisture content, and desired whiteness.

Milling Machine Components and Adjustments

Key components you must know and maintain:

  • Rubber rolls (dehusker): the gap and differential speed determine husking efficiency. Worn rolls cause excessive breakage and unhusked paddy carryover.
  • Abrasive stones: check diameter, flatness, and dressing. A worn stone increases broken grains and power consumption.
  • Screen cylinders: perforations must be clear; blocked screens cause pressure build-up and breakage.
  • Pressure gate / outlet resistance: controls whitening degree and residence time. Too much pressure = breakage; too little = under-milled rice.
  • Air aspiration system: removes bran and cools the milling chamber. Insufficient airflow leads to overheating and quality loss.
  • Feed rate control: must match machine capacity. Overfeeding chokes the mill; underfeeding reduces efficiency and increases broken grains.

Capacity and Efficiency Calculations

Use these formulas to evaluate and compare mill performance. They are the basis for investment decisions and for monitoring daily operations.

Table 1: Key Rice Milling Performance Indicators and Formulas
Indicator Formula Typical African Benchmark
Head Rice Recovery (HRR) (Weight of head rice Ã· Weight of paddy) Ã 100 50â65% (multi-pass); 35â50% (one-pass)
Total Milling Recovery (Weight of milled rice Ã· Weight of paddy) Ã 100 60â70%
Broken Grain Percentage (Weight of broken Ã· Weight of milled rice) Ã 100 <10% (multi-pass); 20â35% (one-pass)
Milling Capacity Tonnes of paddy milled per hour 0.5â5 t/h (SME); 5â20 t/h (industrial)
Milling Efficiency (Actual output Ã· Rated capacity) Ã 100 75â90%
Specific Energy Consumption kWh per tonne of paddy milled 25â45 kWh/t (multi-pass)

Source: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Milling" technical notes; FAO, Rice Milling (1990); Africa Rice Center (AfricaRice), Rice Processing in Africa training materials.

Table 2: Comparative Economics of One-Pass vs Multi-Pass Milling (Illustrative, 2 t/h Mill)
Parameter One-Pass Mill Multi-Pass Mill
Capital cost (USD) 8,000â15,000 60,000â150,000
Head rice recovery 40â50% 55â65%
Broken grain % 25â35% 5â12%
Market price premium Low (broken rice market) High (urban/supermarket)
Labour requirement 2â3 operators 5â10 operators
Maintenance cost Low Moderateâhigh
Payback period 1â2 years 3â5 years

Source: Africa Rice Center (AfricaRice) and FAO post-harvest loss studies; indicative figures for East and West African SME mills, adjusted for 2024 equipment prices.

â  SAFETY WARNING â DUST AND MACHINERY HAZARDS

Rice milling generates fine bran and husk dust that is highly combustible. Dust explosions have destroyed mills in Nigeria, Tanzania, and Senegal. Always install dust extraction and collection systems, avoid open flames near milling areas, and ground all electrical equipment. Never reach into a running dehusker, whitener, or auger to clear a blockage â isolate power and lock out before maintenance. Rubber roll dehuskers and abrasive stones can cause severe hand injuries. Wear dust masks, safety glasses, and hearing protection. Ensure all guards are in place and that only trained operators adjust pressure gates or feed rates.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Check paddy moisture before milling â 14% is ideal; too dry causes breakage, too wet clogs the mill.
  2. Verify rubber roll gap and condition daily; replace worn rolls to prevent unhusked paddy carryover.
  3. Inspect abrasive stones for flatness and diameter; dress or replace as needed.
  4. Clean screen cylinders and aspiration ducts every shift to prevent pressure build-up and overheating.
  5. Adjust pressure gate gradually and monitor broken grain percentage after each change.
  6. Record input paddy weight, output head rice, and broken rice for every batch to track HRR and efficiency.
  7. Monitor specific energy consumption (kWh/t); a sudden rise signals worn parts or misadjustment.
  8. Follow lock-out/tag-out procedures and enforce dust control and PPE use at all times.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Rice Milling (Agricultural Services Bulletin) â full technical reference on milling systems, equipment, and quality.
  • IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank â Milling â practical guides on milling process, equipment, and quality assessment.
  • Africa Rice Center (AfricaRice) â regional training materials and post-harvest research for African rice value chains.
  • FAO Policy Support â Post-Harvest and Agro-Processing â policy and investment resources for rice processing in Africa.
  • ISO / National Standards Bodies â search for rice milling machinery safety and quality standards applicable in your country.

quiz.q: What is a one-pass milling system?
options: A) A system that uses one machine to dehusk, whiten, and polish in one go
B) A system that requires paddy to be milled twice
C) A system that only removes husk
D) A system that uses multiple machines for each step
quiz.explanation: One-pass systems use a single machine to perform all milling steps in one pass.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an advantage of multi-pass milling systems?
quiz.explanation: Multi-pass systems separate tasks, leading to less breakage and higher head rice yield.

quiz.q: What is a typical capacity of a small one-pass mill?
quiz.explanation: Small one-pass mills, like Engelberg types, typically process 200-500 kg per hour.

quiz.q: Why is proper paddy cleaning important before milling?
options: A) It increases the weight of rice
B) It reduces wear and breakage
C) It makes the rice whiter
D) It speeds up the milling process
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes stones and straw that can damage machines and cause broken grains.

quiz.q: Which power source is common for a one-pass mill in rural Africa?
quiz.explanation: Diesel engines are commonly used where grid electricity is unreliable or unavailable.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between vertical and horizontal milling machines?
options: A) Vertical machines use gravity to move grain
B) Horizontal machines are always smaller
C) Vertical machines require more power
D) Horizontal machines cannot polish rice
quiz.explanation: Vertical machines rely on gravity to feed grain downward, while horizontal machines use mechanical conveyance.

quiz.q: Which type of milling machine is generally more space-efficient?
quiz.explanation: Vertical machines take up less floor space due to their upright design.

quiz.q: What is a common example of a vertical milling machine?
quiz.explanation: The VTA (vertical abrasive) whitener is a common vertical machine used in medium mills.

quiz.q: Why do horizontal milling machines often require more power?
options: B) They push grain horizontally against gravity
C) They use more abrasive stones
D) They need to heat the rice
quiz.explanation: Horizontal machines must move grain horizontally, requiring more energy than gravity-fed vertical machines.

quiz.q: Which combination is commonly used in African mills?
options: A) Vertical dehusker and horizontal whitener
quiz.explanation: A vertical rubber roll dehusker followed by a horizontal friction whitener is a typical setup.

quiz.q: What is abrasive whitening?
options: A) Using friction between grains to remove bran
B) Using a rotating abrasive stone to scrape bran
C) Using water to wash off bran
D) Using air to blow off bran
quiz.explanation: Abrasive whitening uses a rotating stone or roller to scrape the bran layer off the grain.

quiz.q: Which whitening technique produces less broken kernels?
options: D) Neither, breakage depends on paddy
quiz.explanation: Abrasive whitening is gentler and typically results in fewer broken grains than friction whitening.

quiz.q: What is a common problem with friction whitening?
options: A) It removes too little bran
D) It works only on long grain
quiz.explanation: Friction whitening generates heat, which can cause broken grains if not controlled.

quiz.q: How often should abrasive stones be dressed?
quiz.explanation: Abrasive stones should be dressed every 100-200 hours to maintain sharpness and milling efficiency.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test to check degree of milling?
quiz.explanation: Rubbing a few grains with your fingers can indicate if bran is easily removed or if grain cracks.

quiz.q: What is the function of the pressure gate in a milling machine?
options: A) To feed paddy into the machine
B) To control the resistance and degree of milling
quiz.explanation: The pressure gate adjusts the resistance inside the milling chamber, affecting how much bran is removed.

quiz.q: What happens if the pressure gate is closed too much?
options: B) More whole grains are produced
quiz.explanation: Excessive pressure increases friction and heat, leading to more broken grains.

quiz.q: Why is belt tension important in a rice mill?
options: A) It affects the color of rice
B) Loose belts reduce speed and milling quality
C) Tight belts increase broken rice
quiz.explanation: Loose belts slip, reducing roller speed and leading to poor milling and lower capacity.

quiz.q: How often should screens be inspected?
quiz.explanation: Screens should be checked every 100 hours for wear, as holes can enlarge and let whole grains escape.

quiz.q: What is the recommended clearance between roller and screen for abrasive whiteners?
quiz.explanation: A clearance of 10-15 mm is typical for abrasive whiteners to allow proper milling without excessive breakage.

quiz.q: What is a process flow diagram (PFD)?
options: A) A diagram of machine parts
B) A drawing showing steps from paddy to polished rice
C) A chart of electricity usage
D) A map of the mill layout
quiz.explanation: A PFD illustrates the sequence of processes and equipment in a rice mill.

quiz.q: In a typical multi-pass mill PFD, what comes after dehusking?
quiz.explanation: After dehusking, a paddy separator removes unhulled paddy from brown rice.

quiz.q: Why is a PFD useful for identifying bottlenecks?
options: A) It shows the cost of each machine
B) It shows capacity at each stage
quiz.explanation: By showing the flow and capacity of each step, a PFD helps spot stages that limit overall throughput.

quiz.q: What by-product is often used as fuel in African rice mills?
quiz.explanation: Husk is commonly burned to generate heat for the mill or to make briquettes.

quiz.q: What is head rice yield?
options: A) Total milled rice divided by paddy weight
B) Weight of whole kernels divided by paddy weight
C) Weight of bran divided by paddy weight
D) Weight of husk divided by paddy weight
quiz.explanation: Head rice yield is the percentage of whole kernels obtained from paddy.

quiz.q: If you mill 100 kg paddy and get 55 kg head rice, what is the head rice yield?
quiz.explanation: Head rice yield = (55/100) Ã 100 = 55%.

quiz.q: What moisture content is ideal for milling paddy?
quiz.explanation: Paddy should be dried to 12-14% moisture for best milling results, reducing breakage.

quiz.q: What is milling recovery?
options: A) Head rice divided by paddy
B) Total milled rice divided by paddy
quiz.explanation: Milling recovery is the total milled rice (head + broken) as a percentage of paddy weight.

quiz.q: How can you improve head rice yield?
quiz.explanation: Keeping abrasive stones sharp ensures efficient bran removal with less breakage.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record daily milling data?
options: B) To track efficiency and identify improvements
quiz.explanation: Recording input and output helps calculate efficiency and spot trends for improvement.
